# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" (statutory term, 8 U.S.C. 1365) in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. The series argues for stronger interior enforcement; copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Prefer federal primary sources (ICE, USSC, GAO, BJS) over secondary analyses.
B3. Counter-research (e.g. Cato's Texas DPS analyses): appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique.
B4. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.
Let me check the archived Brief 13 for format reference.

Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens | United States Sentencing Commission 

 Skip to main content

 Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens

 Of the 66,662 cases reported to the Commission in fiscal year 2025, 28,886 involved non-U.S. citizens. 1 Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 44% of all individuals sentenced in fiscal year 2025.
 Click the cover for the PDF handout or learn more below.  
 Individual and Offense Characteristics

 94% of non-U.S. citizens sentenced in the federal system were men.

 95% were Hispanic, 2% were Black, 2% were White, and 2% were Other races.

 Their average age was 37 years. 

 92% were illegal aliens, 6% were legal aliens, 1% were extradited aliens, and 1% were unknown status.

 66% were from Mexico, 10% from Honduras, 8% from Guatemala, 3% from El Salvador, 3% from the Dominican Republic, and 11% originated from other countries.

 The most common guidelines under which non-U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Immigration (79%); Drug Trafficking (12%); Fraud (3%);  Firearms (2%); Money Laundering (1%); and Administration of Justice (1%). 2 

 59% had little or no prior criminal history (Criminal History Category I); 21% were CHC II;
 13% were CHC III;
 4% were CHC IV;
 2% were CHC V;
 1% were CHC VI.

 The top five districts for sentenced non-U.S. citizens were: Western District of Texas (7,346);
 Southern District of Texas (4,814);
 District of Arizona (2,576);
 District of New Mexico (2,150);
 Southern District of California (747).

 The top five districts where sentenced non-U.S. citizens comprised the highest proportion of the overall caseloads were: District of Northern Mariana Islands (82%);
 Western District of Texas (80%);
 District of New Mexico (80%);
 Southern District of Texas (72%);
 District of Arizona (66%).

 Punishment
 The average sentence for non-U.S. citizens was 21 months. 3 

 97% were sentenced to prison.

 9% were convicted of an offense carrying a mandatory minimum penalty.

 Sentences Relative to the Guideline Range
 79% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were under the Guidelines Manual. 63% were within the guideline range.

 10% were Early Disposition Program (EDP) departures. 4 The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 3% were substantial assistance departures. The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 2% were some other downward departure. The average sentence reduction was 42%. 

 Less than 1% were upward departures. The average sentence increase was 106%. 

 21% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were variances. 15% were downward variances. The average sentence reduction was 39%. 

 6% were upward variances. The average sentence increase was 65%. 

 The average guideline minimum and the average sentence imposed have fluctuated over the past five years. The average guideline minimum was 33 months in fiscal year 2021 and 25 months in fiscal year 2025.

 The average sentence imposed was 25 months in fiscal year 2021 and 21 months in fiscal year 2025.

 1 Cases with incomplete sentencing information were excluded from the analysis.
 2  The most common guidelines under which U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Drug Trafficking (36%); Firearms (21%); Fraud (12%); Immigration (7%); Child Pornography (4%); Sexual Abuse (4%);  and Robbery (3%).
 3  The average sentence for U.S. citizens was 71 months.
 4  “Early Disposition Program" (or EDP) departures are departures where the government sought a sentence below the guideline range because the defendant participated in the government’s Early Disposition Program, through which cases are resolved in an expedited manner. See USSG §5K3.1.
 SOURCE: United States Sentencing Commission, FY 2021 through FY 2025 Datafiles, USSCFY21-USSCFY25.

Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org 

 Skip to main content 

 FactCheck .org ® 

 A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center 

 This article is available in both English and Español 
 English 
 Español 

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

 A: No. An Ohio mental health center rebutted false online rumors that Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, had been there as a patient. Talarico said he was off the campaign trail for several days in early October while recovering from the flu at his Texas home.

Trump and allies mischaracterize data on immigrants with criminal convictions. Here's context on what the numbers actually show. - CBS News 

 Watch CBS News

 In recent days, former President Donald Trump and his allies have cited recently released data on immigrants with criminal convictions to claim that the Biden administration has allowed tens of thousands of criminals into the U.S., including thousands of murderers and sexual offenders.
 "Kamala should immediately cancel her News Conference because it was just revealed that 13,000 convicted murderers entered our Country during her three and a half year period as Border Czar," Trump wrote in a social media post Friday. "Also currently in our Country because of her are 15,811 migrants convicted of rape and sexual assault."
 Trump was presumably citing a letter U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recently shared with Texas Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales. The letter, which Gonzalez published on Friday, contained figures on immigrants with criminal records being tracked by ICE but not detained by the agency. Trump and right-wing figures have mischaracterized the data by claiming that everyone on the list entered under the Biden administration and remains freely in the U.S.
 The bottom line is that many of the convicted criminals described in the letter have been in the U.S. for a long time, before the Biden administration took office, according to government data and officials. Some are still in federal or state custody serving criminal sentences and are likely to be arrested by ICE. And others cannot be deported because their home countries won't take them back or they received legal relief from deportation in immigration court.
 What does the data actually show?
 The letter ICE sent to Gonzales broke down the number of immigrants with criminal convictions or charges in the agency's "non-detained docket."
 ICE detains immigrants who are deportable because they are in the U.S. illegally, after crossing a border unlawfully or overstaying a visa, or because they lost their legal right to be in the country after being convicted of certain crimes. Under U.S. law, this can happen to green card holders and other legal immigrants who commit certain crimes.

 Detainees talk on telephones at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in Adelanto, California, on Aug. 28, 2019. 

 Chris Carlson / AP

 While the agency runs detention facilities to hold immigrants awaiting deportation, ICE also oversees a "non-detained docket" to monitor the cases of immigrants who are facing deportation proceedings before an immigration judge, without being detained by the agency.

 The number of non-detained docket cases has ballooned under the Biden administration, fueled by the release of millions of migrants from the U.S.-Mexico border in recent years. ICE is currently tracking roughly 7.7 million non-detained cases, up from 3.3 million in fiscal year 2020 , according to agency data provided by a U.S. official. The agency has 41,000 detention beds funded by Congress — not nearly enough to detain everyone facing removal proceedings.
 The letter to Gonzales shows that out of millions of cases, ICE's non-detained docket includes 425,000 immigrants with criminal convictions and 222,000 with pending criminal charges. The list includes 13,099 immigrants convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault.
 Not every person arrived under Biden
 Not every immigrant with a criminal record on ICE's non-detained docket arrived in the U.S. under President Biden's tenure. In fact, official figures indicate many of them have been here for years — if not decades.
 In June 2021, just several months into the Biden administration, there were 405,786 convicted criminals in ICE's non-detained docket, according to agency data . In August 2016, during the Obama administration, there were 368,574 convicted criminals in ICE's non-detained docket, according to data published by the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General.

 "The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration," DHS spokesperson Luis Miranda said in a statement to CBS News.
 Some remain incarcerated in federal or local facilities
 While they're not in ICE's custody, many of the convicted criminals or criminal suspects in the agency's non-detained docket are still incarcerated in federal, state or local custody serving their criminal sentences or awaiting trial, U.S. officials told CBS News. But since ICE is tracking their cases, they are technically part of its non-detained docket. 
 The docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners," said Miranda, the DHS spokesperson.
 ICE expects to arrest, detain and deport those convicted of serious crimes once they finish their criminal sentences, a U.S. official said. Those immigrants have long been considered a priority for arrest by ICE, including under Biden administration policy , which instructs the agency to focus their efforts on detaining public safety threats, national security risks and recent border crossers. 
 That being said, ICE efforts to arrest immigrants accused or convicted of crimes are often frustrated by jurisdictions with so-called "sanctuary" policies that limit local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Some communities, for example, do not honor requests from ICE to hold individuals longer so the agency can pick them up and take them into custody.
 Others cannot be deported
 Some immigrants with criminal records are able to remain in the U.S. due to diplomatic or legal reasons.
 Certain countries, like China, Cuba and Venezuela, limit or outright reject the return of their citizens from the U.S. and the Supreme Court has largely banned indefinite detention in these cases through a 2001 ruling . That means that ICE sometimes has to release immigrants who have been ordered deported by a judge, often because of a criminal conviction, simply because their home country won't accept them.

 Additionally, some immigrants, even those convicted of serious crimes, can have their deportation deferred if immigration judges determine they would likely be tortured or persecuted in their home countries. That's because the U.S. has binding legal obligations to offer protection to certain foreigners under the United Nations Convention Against Torture and the United Nations Refugee Protocol , which is implemented through a little-known benefit known as withholding of removal.

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics

 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers enforce immigration laws within the interior to preserve national security and public safety.

 ERO manages all aspects of the immigration enforcement process, including the identification, arrest, detention and removal of aliens who are subject to removal or are unlawfully present in the United States.

 Like all law enforcement agencies, ERO officers prioritize their enforcement actions based on agency and department priorities, funding and capacity. ERO operations are flexible enough to allow its officers to respond to events such as spikes in border crossings, modifications to U.S. laws, pandemics, and natural disasters at home and abroad.

 The following dashboards present for the first time information and trends in arrests, detentions, removals and alternatives to detention as of December 31, 2024. 

 The dashboards will be updated quarterly.

We will continue to evaluate and enhance how the agency communicates measurable data to best inform how our officers and special agents perform their law enforcement missions in accordance with departmental and agency priorities.” — ICE Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director Patrick J. Lechleitner

 Arrest Statistics
 ERO enforces laws by arresting immigration violators in the interior of the United States. It relies on statutory law enforcement authority to identify and arrest aliens who may present threats to national security or public safety, or who otherwise undermine the integrity of U.S. immigration laws. ERO uses targeted, intelligence-driven operations to prioritize its enforcement actions in ways that help protect communities nationwide. While ERO primarily conducts administrative arrests of aliens it has probable cause to believe are removable from the United States, it also has the authority to execute criminal arrest warrants and initiate prosecutions for criminal activity, including immigration-related crimes. ERO officers assigned to task forces also help target and apprehend foreign fugitives in the United States who are wanted for crimes here and abroad by working with domestic and international partners.

 For fiscal years 2021 and 2022, this category also includes individuals apprehended while attempting to unlawfully enter the United States after January 1, 2021.

 ERO arrests over time: Historically, ERO most commonly arrests immigration violators with convictions involving DUI, drug possession, assault and criminal (non-civil) traffic offenses such as hit-and-run or leaving the scene of an accident.
 Arrests by Area of Responsibility (AOR): ERO has 24 field offices, which are geographic areas of responsibility , around the country, each headed by a field office director.

The ERO Headquarters Custody Management and ICE Health Service Corps divisions help officers in the field manage the detained population and ensure detained aliens’ health and safety, ensure compliance with ICE’s detention standards, and provide medical care — including mental health care — to detained individuals.

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act 

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act

 ICE’s 287(g) Program
 The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 added Section 287(g) to the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), authorizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to delegate state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.
 The Program enhances the safety and security of our nation’s communities by allowing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) to partner with state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies to identify and remove criminal aliens who are amenable to removal from the United States.
 ICE recognizes the importance of its relationships with law enforcement partners—including state and local agencies—to carry out its critical mission.
 Through the delegation of specified immigration officer duties, the program allows ICE to enhance collaboration with state and local law enforcement partners to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.
 What’s in It for Your Law Enforcement Agency?
 The 287(g) Program benefits state and local law enforcement agencies in several ways — but most notably, it helps you keep your community safe from potentially dangerous criminal aliens. Your law enforcement officers will get access to ICE resources and training. ICE covers the cost of training (see the later section, “287(g) Training Available to State and Local Law Enforcement,” for more information).
 Your agency or office may be eligible for the Department of Justice’s State Criminal Alien Assistance Program . This Department of Justice program administers SCAAP awards and provides federal funding to states and political subdivisions of states, including municipalities that incur costs for incarcerating certain criminal aliens. This is entirely separate from the 287(g) program. 
 ICE 287(g) Program Map

 287(g) Program Models
 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations operates three 287(g) models:
 The  Jail Enforcement Model allows designated immigration officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.
 The  Task Force Model  enhances public safety and national security by allowing designated immigration officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.
 The Warrant Service Officer Model allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their custody.
 How Can Your Agency Participate in the ICE 287(g) Program?
 On January 20, 2025, President Donald J. Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion . This EO requires ICE to authorize State and local law enforcement officials, as the Secretary of Homeland Security determines are qualified and appropriate, under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to the maximum extent permitted by law. Several states, including but not limited to Georgia and Florida, have passed, or are considering, State legislation mandating law enforcement agencies (LEAs) seek out or enter into memorandums of agreement (MOA) with ICE pursuant to a partnership under the 287(g) Program.
 Participation in the 287(g) Program is limited to LEAs only. LEAs interested in participating in the 287(g) Program must sign an MOA with ICE. LEAs will nominate officers to participate in the 287(g) Program. Nominees must possess U.S. citizenship, complete and pass a background investigation, and have knowledge of and have enforced laws and regulations related to law enforcement activities at their jurisdictions. Task Force Model nominees must also have at least two (2) years of total law enforcement officer experience. Nominees will receive training at the expense of ICE related to the immigration duties pertinent to the applicable MOA.
 LEAs interested in becoming a law enforcement partner under the 287(g) Program must submit a signed MOA to ICE at ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . These forms can be found below.

 Please click on the applicable MOA (fillable), complete and sign in its entirety, and email back to the 287(g) program team at: ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov .

 ICE has several resources, including this page, that can help you show your chief, sheriff or team all the benefits the 287(g) Program provides. From here, you can also download and print ICE’s:
 287(g) fact sheet.

 If you have any questions about participating in the ICE 287(g) program, how to complete the necessary forms, what is required, or would like additional information, please do not hesitate to email ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov ; your inquiry will be promptly answered within one business day.

 New ICE data reveals who federal agents are detaining in immigration raids 01:57 Get more news on Share Add NBC News to Google June 25, 2025, 6:00 AM EDT By Julia Ainsley and Laura Strickler After six months of aggressive immigration enforcement and promises to focus on deporting violent criminals, the Trump administration has arrested and detained a small fraction of the undocumented immigrants already known to Immigration and Customs Enforcement as having been convicted of sexual assault and homicide, internal ICE data obtained by NBC News shows.
 The data is a tally of every person booked by ICE from Oct. 1 through May 31, part of which was during the Biden administration. It shows a total of 185,042 people arrested and booked into ICE facilities during that time; 65,041 of them have been convicted of crimes. The most common categories of crimes they committed were immigration and traffic offenses.
 Almost half of the people currently in ICE custody have neither been convicted of nor charged with any crime, other ICE data shows .
 Law enforcement officials escort a suspect during a raid of an apartment complex in east Denver on Feb. 5. David Zalubowski / AP file Last fall, ICE told Congress that 13,099 people convicted of homicide and 15,811 people convicted of sexual assault were on its non-detained docket, meaning it knew who they were but did not have them in custody. A spokesperson said at the time that ICE had some information about but did not know the exact whereabouts of all the immigrants on the non-detained docket and that some could have left the United States or could be in prison.
 Running for president at the time, Donald Trump used those figures to criticize his opponent, Vice President Kamala Harris.
 “These are hard, tough, vicious criminals that are free to roam in our country,” Trump said at a campaign stop in Michigan.

*Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14*

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- Federal data put 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, along with 425,431 convicted criminals in all. These are offenders ICE has identified and does not hold, a standing confession that interior enforcement runs on capacity, not on public safety.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of them were illegal aliens. By FY2025 the noncitizen share of the federal docket reached 44%.
- Sanctuary policies are measurable: New York alone refused 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, detainers that covered aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides. ## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

Laken Riley was 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens when Jose Antonio Ibarra attacked and killed her in February 2024. Ibarra, an illegal alien from Venezuela, had crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and been paroled into the interior. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child; he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. In November 2024 a Georgia judge convicted him of Riley's murder and sentenced him to life without parole.

Nothing about that record was unpredictable. Every link in the chain was a policy choice, and the federal government's own data show how many similar cases it is carrying.

The scale is documented by ICE itself. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. The convictions included 13,099 homicides and 15,811 sexual assaults. "Non-detained" means what it says: these are people ICE has processed and identified but does not hold. Some are serving state or federal sentences and will be released one day; others are in the community; others ICE simply cannot find.

The docket's size is the product of decades of under-resourced interior enforcement. The Congressional Research Service reports that ICE's non-detained docket reached 7.3 million cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including roughly 1.6 million aliens with final orders of removal. Enforcement against that backlog is arithmetic, not rhetoric: according to internal ICE data obtained by NBC News, from Oct. 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025 the agency arrested 752 people convicted of homicide, at most 6% of the known homicide convicts on its own docket, and 1,693 convicted of sexual assault, at most 11%. Even an administration committed to removing criminal aliens cannot arrest its way through the backlog with the beds and officers Congress has funded.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

Laken Riley was 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens in February 2024 when Jose Antonio Ibarra attacked and killed her. Ibarra, an illegal alien from Venezuela, had crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child, and he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. A Georgia judge convicted Ibarra of Riley's murder in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

Every link in that chain was a policy choice. And the federal government's own numbers show how many more cases like it the system is carrying.

The scale is documented by ICE itself. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions. "Non-detained" means what it says: not in ICE custody. Some of those convicted are serving sentences in other jurisdictions' prisons and will walk out one day; others are in the community; others ICE cannot find.

The docket is the arithmetic of decades of under-resourced interior enforcement. The Congressional Research Service reports that it stood at 7.3 million cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including roughly 1.6 million aliens with final orders of removal. Working that backlog is arithmetic too. Internal ICE data obtained by NBC News show that from Oct. 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025, the agency arrested 752 people convicted of homicide, at most 6% of the known homicide convicts on its own docket, and 1,693 convicted of sexual assault, at most 11% of them. Even an administration committed to removing criminal aliens cannot detain the criminal docket with the beds and officers Congress has funded.

## 2. One in Three Federal Offenders, and Rising

The same pattern appears at the front end of the system, in federal sentencing. United States Sentencing Commission data show that non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, 21,304 of 61,678. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens.

The share is climbing. In FY2025, 28,886 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 44% of all individuals sentenced that year, and 92% of them were illegal aliens.

Nor is the federal docket composed only of immigration offenses. Noncitizens accounted for 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking offenders sentenced in FY2024, nearly one in five.

Enforcement capacity, meanwhile, spent years moving the other way. The Government Accountability Office found that the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to 21,500 (GAO-24-107598, October 2024). The country did not run out of criminal aliens. It ran out of immigration enforcement.

## 3. What the Texas Record Actually Shows

Texas is one of the few states that records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, and for a decade advocates have leaned on Texas Department of Public Safety data to claim that illegal aliens offend at lower rates than the native born. The claim is an artifact of how status is recorded, not of how crime is distributed.

Texas ascertains the immigration status of many offenders only after they are in custody, sometimes years into a sentence. Analysts who divide the convictions of identified illegal aliens by a population estimate treat the unidentified remainder as native born and systematically understate illegal-alien criminality. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies who re-examined the DPS records conclude that once delayed identification is accounted for, illegal aliens are convicted at higher rates than native-born Americans for serious crimes in Texas, including homicide and sexual assault (Kennedy, Richwine and Camarota, October 2022).

Texas is not evidence that criminal aliens are rare. It is evidence of what a state can learn when it asks the question.

## 4. Detainers Refused, With the Bodies Counted

Ibarra was released by New York police before ICE could lodge a detainer. That pattern is now quantified in federal data.

The Department of Homeland Security reported on Oct. 12, 2026 that New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026. Those detainers covered aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicides, 132 kidnappings, 1,017 sexual offenses, 9,502 assaults, 2,198 weapons offenses and 4,324 dangerous drug cases. New York is the example, not the exception. ICE records produced to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2026 show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022 through Feb. 6, 2025, 52% of them in California alone (13,025), plus more than 1,400 instances in which jails failed to notify ICE of a release at all.

Cooperation, by contrast, compounds. Under Executive Order 14159, ICE has expanded its 287(g) partnerships, which deputize state and local officers to enforce immigration law, by 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025, to 2,246 active agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026. By Oct. 15, 2026, ICE had signed 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two territories. Every one of those agreements is a memorandum, not a statute, and a future administration could cancel it.

## Recommendations

1. Fund criminal-alien detention. Appropriate detention capacity dedicated to the non-detained docket's criminal cases, beginning with the 13,099 homicide and 15,811 sexual assault convictions ICE has already identified, and direct DHS to prioritize them.

2. Condition federal funds on detainer compliance. Make law enforcement and criminal justice grants to state and local governments contingent on honoring ICE detainers and providing notice of release dates.

3. Expand and protect 287(g). Fund training and equipment for participating agencies, require DHS to offer agreements to every state, and shield participating agencies from state-law retaliation.

4. Require public reporting. Direct DHS to publish quarterly the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, detainers issued and declined by jurisdiction, and every release of a criminal alien from custody.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute | Washington | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- ICE data reported to Congress on Sept. 25, 2024 place 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault on the agency's non-detained docket, alongside 425,431 convicted criminals in all. These are offenders the federal government has identified and does not hold.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. By FY2025 the noncitizen share of the federal sentencing docket reached 44%.
- Refused detainers are counted in federal data: New York state alone declined 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, covering aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program and require public reporting of criminal-alien releases.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

Laken Riley was 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens in February 2024 when Jose Antonio Ibarra attacked and killed her. Ibarra, an illegal alien from Venezuela, had crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child, and he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. A Georgia judge convicted Ibarra of Riley's murder in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

Every link in that chain was a policy choice. And the federal government's own numbers show how many more cases like it the system is carrying.

The scale is documented by ICE itself. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions. "Non-detained" means what it says: not in ICE custody. Some of those convicted are serving sentences in other jurisdictions' prisons and will walk out one day; others are in the community; others ICE cannot find.

The docket is the arithmetic of decades of under-resourced interior enforcement. The Congressional Research Service reports that it stood at 7.3 million cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including roughly 1.6 million aliens with final orders of removal. Working that backlog is arithmetic too. Internal ICE data obtained by NBC News show that from Oct. 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025, the agency arrested 752 people convicted of homicide, at most 6% of the known homicide convicts on its own docket, and 1,693 convicted of sexual assault, at most 11% of them. Even an administration committed to removing criminal aliens cannot detain the criminal docket with the beds and officers Congress has funded.

## 2. One in Three Federal Offenders, and Rising

The same pattern appears at the front end of the system, in federal sentencing. United States Sentencing Commission data show that non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, 21,304 of 61,678. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens.

The share is climbing. In FY2025, 28,886 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 44% of all individuals sentenced that year, and 92% of them were illegal aliens.

Nor is the federal docket composed only of immigration offenses. Noncitizens accounted for 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking offenders sentenced in FY2024, nearly one in five.

Enforcement capacity, meanwhile, spent years moving the other way. The Government Accountability Office found that the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to 21,500 (GAO-24-107598, October 2024). The country did not run out of criminal aliens. It ran out of immigration enforcement.

Hmm — "The country did not run out of criminal aliens. It ran out of immigration enforcement." Nice persuasive line. Accurate? The 27% decline in noncitizens sentenced FY18→FY23 reflects fewer prosecutions; "ran out of immigration enforcement" is argumentative framing, fine for a brief.

## 3. What the Texas Record Actually Shows

Texas is one of the few states that records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, and for a decade advocates have leaned on Texas Department of Public Safety data to claim that illegal aliens offend at lower rates than the native born. The claim is an artifact of how status is recorded, not of how crime is distributed.

Texas ascertains the immigration status of many offenders only after they are in custody, sometimes years into a sentence. Analysts who divide the convictions of identified illegal aliens by a population estimate treat the unidentified remainder as native born and systematically understate illegal-alien criminality. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies who re-examined the DPS records conclude that once delayed identification is accounted for, illegal aliens are convicted at higher rates than native-born Americans for serious crimes in Texas, including homicide and sexual assault (Kennedy, Richwine and Camarota, October 2022).

Texas is not evidence that criminal aliens are rare. It is evidence of what a state can learn when it asks the question.

## 4. Detainers Refused, With the Bodies Counted

Ibarra was released by New York police before ICE could lodge a detainer. That pattern is now quantified in federal data.

The Department of Homeland Security reported on Oct. 12, 2026 that New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026. Those detainers covered aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicides, 132 kidnappings, 1,017 sexual offenses, 9,502 assaults, 2,198 weapons offenses and 4,324 dangerous drug cases. New York is the example, not the exception. ICE records produced to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2026 show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022 through Feb. 6, 2025, 52% of them in California alone (13,025), plus more than 1,400 instances in which jails failed to notify ICE of a release at all.

Cooperation, by contrast, compounds. Under Executive Order 14159, ICE has expanded its 287(g) partnerships, which deputize state and local officers to enforce immigration law, by 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025, to 2,246 active agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026. By Oct. 15, 2026, ICE had signed 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two territories. Every one of those agreements is a memorandum, not a statute, and a future administration could cancel it.

## Recommendations

1. Fund criminal-alien detention. Appropriate detention capacity dedicated to the non-detained docket's criminal cases, beginning with the 13,099 homicide and 15,811 sexual assault convictions ICE has already identified, and direct DHS to prioritize them.

2. Condition federal funds on detainer compliance. Make law enforcement and criminal justice grants to state and local governments contingent on honoring ICE detainers and providing notice of release dates.

3. Expand and protect 287(g). Fund training and equipment for participating agencies, require DHS to offer agreements to every state, and shield participating agencies from state-law retaliation.

4. Require public reporting. Direct DHS to publish quarterly the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, detainers issued and declined by jurisdiction, and every release of a criminal alien from custody.

**Washington Think Tank: Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers on ICE's Non-Detained Docket; "Congress Can Reverse This"**

{"content": "# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute, Washington | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- ICE data reported to Congress on Sept. 25, 2024 placed 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault on the agency's non-detained docket, alongside 425,431 convicted criminals in all. These are offenders the federal government has identified by name and does not hold.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. By FY2025 the noncitizen share of the federal sentencing docket had reached 44%.
- Refused detainers are now counted in federal data: New York state alone declined 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, covering aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program, and require public reporting of criminal-alien releases.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

Laken Riley was 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens in February 2024 when Jose Antonio Ibarra attacked and killed her. Ibarra, an illegal alien from Venezuela, had crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child, and he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. A Georgia judge convicted Ibarra of Riley's murder in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

Every link in that chain was a policy choice. The federal government's own numbers show how many more cases like it the system is carrying.

The scale is documented by ICE itself. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions. "Non-detained" means what it says: not in ICE custody. Some of those convicted are serving sentences elsewhere and will walk out one day. Others are in the community. Others ICE cannot find. The agency produced the figures only because a congressman asked; there is no schedule for publishing them again.

The docket is the arithmetic of decades of under-resourced interior enforcement. The Congressional Research Service reports that it stood at 7.3 million cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including roughly 1.6 million aliens with final orders of removal. Working the criminal part of that backlog is arithmetic too. Internal ICE data obtained by NBC News show that from Oct. 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025, the agency arrested 752 people convicted of homicide, at most 6% of the known homicide convicts on its own docket, and 1,693 convicted of sexual assault, at most 11% of them. Even an administration committed to removing criminal aliens cannot detain the criminal docket with the beds and officers Congress has funded.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences, and Rising

The same pattern appears at the front end of the system. United States Sentencing Commission data show non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024: 21,304 people. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens.

The share is climbing. In FY2025, 28,886 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 44% of all individuals sentenced that year, and 92% of them were illegal aliens.

Nor is the federal docket made up only of immigration cases. Noncitizens accounted for 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking offenders sentenced in FY2024, nearly one in five.

Enforcement capacity, meanwhile, spent years moving the other way. The Government Accountability Office found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500 (GAO-24-107598, October 2024). The country did not run out of criminal aliens. It ran out of immigration enforcement.

## 3. What the Texas Record Actually Shows

Texas keeps the country's most complete record of the immigration status of people it arrests and convicts, and for a decade advocates have leaned on Texas Department of Public Safety data to claim that illegal aliens offend at lower rates than the native born. That claim is an artifact of how status is recorded, not of how crime is distributed.

Texas ascertains the immigration status of many offenders only after they are in custody, sometimes years into a sentence. Analyses that divide the convictions of identified illegal aliens by a population estimate treat the unidentified remainder as native born and systematically understate illegal-alien criminality. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies who re-examined the DPS records conclude that once delayed identification is accounted for, illegal aliens are convicted at higher rates than the general population for serious crimes in Texas, including homicide and sexual assault (Kennedy, Richwine and Camarota, October 2022).

Texas is not evidence that criminal aliens are rare. It is evidence of what a state can learn about criminal aliens when it asks the question.

## 4. Detainers Refused, With the Bodies Counted

Ibarra was released by New York police before ICE could lodge a detainer. That pattern is now quantified in federal data.

The Department of Homeland Security reported on Oct. 12, 2026 that New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026. Those detainers covered aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicides, 132 kidnappings, 1,017 sexual offenses, 9,502 assaults, 2,198 weapons offenses and 4,324 dangerous drug offenses. New York is the example, not the exception. ICE records produced to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2026 show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022 through Feb. 6, 2025, 52% of them in California alone (13,025), plus more than 1,400 instances in which jails failed to give ICE adequate notification of a release.

Cooperation, by contrast, compounds. Under Executive Order 14159, ICE has grown its 287(g) partnerships, which deputize state and local officers to perform immigration enforcement functions, by 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025, to 2,246 active agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026. By Oct. 15, 2026, ICE had signed 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two territories. Every one of those agreements is a memorandum, not a statute. A future administration could cancel them.

## Recommendations

1. Fund criminal-alien detention. Appropriate detention capacity dedicated to the criminal cases on ICE's non-detained docket, beginning with the 13,099 homicide and 15,811 sexual assault convictions ICE has already identified, and direct DHS to prioritize them.

2. Condition federal funds on detainer compliance. Make law enforcement and criminal justice grants to state and local governments contingent on honoring ICE detainers and providing notice of release dates.

3. Expand and protect 287(g). Fund training and equipment for participating agencies, require DHS to offer agreements to every state, and shield participating agencies from state-law retaliation.

4. Require public reporting. Direct DHS to publish quarterly the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, detainers issued and declined by jurisdiction, and every release of a criminal alien from custody.

---

*Data appendix with full source lines and methodology notes accompanies this brief. Brett Kessler is senior fellow for immigration policy at the Founders' Square Institute.*

{"content": "# Data Appendix: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

Publication-ready tables supporting Brief No. 14, the accompanying fact sheet and social cards. One table per figure used in the brief. Source lines follow the series format (Agency/author, Title, Date, URL). Population, timeframe and methodology notes appear here, per style sheet section B.1, and are kept out of body copy, the fact sheet and cards. Counter-research appears here only, per style sheet section B.3.

## A1. ICE Non-Detained Docket: Criminal Convictions and Charges (data as of July 21, 2024)

| Category | Number |
|---|---|
| Noncitizens on ICE's books with criminal convictions or charges, all dockets | 662,566 |
| Criminal convictions, non-detained docket | 425,431 |
| Pending criminal charges, non-detained docket (approx.) | 222,000 |
| Homicide convictions, non-detained docket | 13,099 |
| Sexual assault convictions, non-detained docket | 15,811 |
| Assault convictions, non-detained docket | 62,231 |
| Pending murder charges, non-detained docket | 1,845 |

**Notes:** The non-detained docket comprises noncitizens with final orders of removal or pending removal proceedings who are not in ICE custody. Per DHS and ICE statements in September and October 2024, the records extend back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the docket includes many noncitizens currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and ICE did not disclose how many. The docket also includes lawful permanent residents and other lawful entrants whose convictions made them removable. ICE stated it does not know the whereabouts of all docket members; some may have left the United States. Approximate figures are as reported from the letter by CBS News and FactCheck.org.

**Used in:** Brief executive summary and Section 1; fact sheet stats 1-3; social cards 1 and 2.

**Source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Patrick J. Lechleitner, Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director), response letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf

## A2. Size of ICE's Non-Detained Docket (data as of Feb. 26, 2026)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Cases on ICE's non-detained docket | 7.3 million |
| Of which, aliens with final orders of removal (est.) | 1.6 million |

**Notes:** The count is a cumulative list of removable aliens, continuously updated; it excludes individuals with confirmed departure or death. Some individuals have been on the docket for decades; others were added recently. A fraction of docket members are enrolled in alternatives to detention.

**Used in:** Brief Section 1; fact sheet stat 8.

**Source:** Congressional Research Service, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD), IF13208.1, 2026, https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/PDF/IF13208/IF13208.1.pdf

## A3. ICE Arrests of Convicted Homicide and Sexual Assault Offenders (Oct. 1, 2024 to May 31, 2025)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Persons booked by ICE with homicide convictions | 752 |
| Share of known docket homicide convicts arrested (upper bound) | 6% |
| Persons booked by ICE with sexual assault convictions | 1,693 |
| Share of known docket sexual assault convicts arrested (upper bound) | 11% |
| Total persons arrested and booked into ICE facilities, period | 185,042 |
| Of which, persons with criminal convictions | 65,041 |

**Notes:** Secondary source (see production note to the Director). The percentages are upper bounds because the docket totals (13,099 homicide convictions, 15,811 sexual assault convictions as of July 21, 2024) may have changed over the counting period. The underlying data are internal ICE records, not a published federal release; DHS disputed the reporting without providing raw figures by category. The most common conviction categories among all book-ins were immigration and traffic offenses.

**Used in:** Brief Section 1.

**Source:** NBC News (Julia Ainsley, Laura Strickler), "Despite promise to remove 'worst of the worst,' ICE has arrested only 6% of known immigrant murderers," June 25, 2025, https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/national-security/promise-remove-worst-worst-ice-arrested-only-6-known-immigrant-murdere-rcna214817

## A4. Federal Sentencing of Non-U.S. Citizens, FY2024 and FY2025 (U.S. Sentencing Commission)

| Measure | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Individuals sentenced, all (reported cases) | 61,678 | 66,662 |

| Second: drug trafficking | 17.6% | 12% |

**Notes:** Sentencing Commission percentages are calculated on individuals sentenced in federal court under the Guidelines Manual; cases with incomplete sentencing information are excluded, and share denominators reflect cases with recorded citizenship (61,342 in FY2024 per Sourcebook Table 9). "Illegal alien" is the Commission's category for persons unlawfully present. Immigration guidelines apply almost exclusively to noncitizens; the noncitizen share of the docket therefore largely reflects immigration prosecutions, and the drug trafficking figures in A5 are the cleaner public safety measure. FY2025 figures postdate the author's source table (FY2024) and are flagged for sign-off.

**Used in:** Brief Section 2 and executive summary; fact sheet stats 4-5; social card 3.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute, Washington | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- ICE data reported to Congress on Sept. 25, 2024 placed 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault on the agency's non-detained docket, alongside 425,431 convicted criminals in all. These are offenders the federal government has identified by name and does not hold.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. By FY2025 the noncitizen share of the federal sentencing docket had reached 44%.
- Refused detainers are now counted in federal data: New York state alone declined 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, covering aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program, and require public reporting of criminal-alien releases.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

Laken Riley was 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens in February 2024 when Jose Antonio Ibarra attacked and killed her. Ibarra, an illegal alien from Venezuela, had crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child, and he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. A Georgia judge convicted Ibarra of Riley's murder in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

Every link in that chain was a policy choice. The federal government's own numbers show how many more cases like it the system is carrying.

The scale is documented by ICE itself. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions. "Non-detained" means what it says: not in ICE custody. Some of those convicted are serving sentences elsewhere and will walk out one day. Others are in the community. Others ICE cannot find. Across ICE's books as a whole, the agency counted 662,566 noncitizens with criminal convictions or charges. The figures were produced only because a congressman asked; there is no schedule for publishing them again.

The docket is the arithmetic of decades of under-resourced interior enforcement. The Congressional Research Service reports that it stood at 7.3 million cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including roughly 1.6 million aliens with final orders of removal. Working the criminal part of that backlog is arithmetic too. Internal ICE data obtained by NBC News show that from Oct. 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025, the agency arrested 752 people convicted of homicide, at most 6% of the known homicide convicts on its own docket, and 1,693 convicted of sexual assault, at most 11% of them. Even an administration committed to removing criminal aliens cannot detain the criminal docket with the beds and officers Congress has funded.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences, and Rising

The same pattern appears at the front end of the system. United States Sentencing Commission data show non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024: 21,304 people. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens.

The share is climbing. In FY2025, 28,886 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 44% of all individuals sentenced that year, and 92% of them were illegal aliens.

Nor is the federal docket made up only of immigration cases. Noncitizens accounted for 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking offenders sentenced in FY2024, nearly one in five.

Enforcement capacity, meanwhile, spent years moving the other way. The Government Accountability Office found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500 (GAO-24-107598, October 2024). The country did not run out of criminal aliens. It ran out of immigration enforcement.

## 3. What the Texas Record Actually Shows

Texas keeps the country's most complete record of the immigration status of people it arrests and convicts, and for a decade advocates have leaned on Texas Department of Public Safety data to claim that illegal aliens offend at lower rates than the native born. That claim is an artifact of how status is recorded, not of how crime is distributed.

Texas ascertains the immigration status of many offenders only after they are in custody, sometimes years into a sentence. Analyses that divide the convictions of identified illegal aliens by a population estimate treat the unidentified remainder as native born and systematically understate illegal-alien criminality. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies who re-examined the DPS records conclude that once delayed identification is accounted for, illegal aliens are convicted at higher rates than the general population for serious crimes in Texas, including homicide and sexual assault (Kennedy, Richwine and Camarota, October 2022).

Texas is not evidence that criminal aliens are rare. It is evidence of what a state can learn about criminal aliens when it asks the question.

## 4. Detainers Refused, With the Bodies Counted

Ibarra was released by New York police before ICE could lodge a detainer. That pattern is now quantified in federal data.

The Department of Homeland Security reported on Oct. 12, 2026 that New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026. Those detainers covered aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicides, 132 kidnappings, 1,017 sexual offenses, 9,502 assaults, 2,198 weapons offenses and 4,324 dangerous drug offenses. New York is the example, not the exception. ICE records produced to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2026 show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022 through Feb. 6, 2025, 52% of them in California alone (13,025), plus more than 1,400 instances in which jails failed to give ICE adequate notification of a release.

Cooperation, by contrast, compounds. Under Executive Order 14159, ICE has grown its 287(g) partnerships, which deputize state and local officers to perform immigration enforcement functions, by 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025, to 2,246 active agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026. By Oct. 15, 2026, ICE had signed 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two territories. New York has moved to stamp cooperation out: a state law signed in May 2026 bars local police departments from partnering or cooperating with ICE, effective Aug. 25, 2026. Every one of the 2,679 agreements is a memorandum, not a statute, and a future administration could cancel them.

## Recommendations

1. Fund criminal-alien detention. Appropriate detention capacity dedicated to the criminal cases on ICE's non-detained docket, beginning with the 13,099 homicide and 15,811 sexual assault convictions ICE has already identified, and direct DHS to prioritize them.

2. Condition federal funds on detainer compliance. Make law enforcement and criminal justice grants to state and local governments contingent on honoring ICE detainers and providing notice of release dates.

3. Expand and protect 287(g). Fund training and equipment for participating agencies, require DHS to offer agreements to every state, and shield participating agencies from state-law retaliation.

4. Require public reporting. Direct DHS to publish quarterly the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, detainers issued and declined by jurisdiction, and every release of a criminal alien from custody.

---

*Data appendix with full source lines and methodology notes accompanies this brief. Brett Kessler is senior fellow for immigration policy at the Founders' Square Institute.*

=== press_release.md ===
# EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE UNTIL 10:00 A.M. ET, TUESDAY, OCT. 27, 2026

## Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers on ICE's Non-Detained Docket; FSI Brief Tells Congress to Fund the Fix

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Founders' Square Institute today releases Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. The brief assembles ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, GAO and DHS data to document the public safety cost of weak interior enforcement.

The brief finds:

- ICE reported to Congress on Sept. 25, 2024 that its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions.
- Non-U.S. citizens were 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024 and 44% in FY2025; 88.7% and 92% of them, respectively, were illegal aliens.
- New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, covering aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides.

"The federal government knows, by name and conviction, of more than thirteen thousand noncitizen killers it does not hold, and from October 2024 through May 2025, ICE arrested at most six percent of them," Kessler said. "That is not a mystery. It is a capacity decision, and Congress can reverse it."

The brief recommends that Congress fund detention capacity dedicated to the criminal cases on ICE's non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement grants on detainer compliance, expand and protect 287(g) partnerships with state and local police, and require DHS to publish quarterly data on the docket and on criminal-alien releases.

Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, with data appendix and fact sheet, is available at [FSI publication URL] on Oct. 27, 2026.

Media contact: [FSI Communications contact]

###

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute, Washington | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- ICE data reported to Congress on Sept. 25, 2024 placed 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault on the agency's non-detained docket, alongside 425,431 convicted criminals in all. These are offenders the federal government has identified by name and does not hold.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. By FY2025 the noncitizen share of the federal sentencing docket had reached 44%.
- Refused detainers are now counted in federal data: New York state alone declined 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, covering aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program, and require public reporting of criminal-alien releases.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

Laken Riley was 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens in February 2024 when Jose Antonio Ibarra attacked and killed her. Ibarra, an illegal alien from Venezuela, had crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child, and he was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. A Georgia judge convicted Ibarra of Riley's murder in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

Every link in that chain was a policy choice. The federal government's own numbers show how many more cases like it the system is carrying.

The scale is documented by ICE itself. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the agency reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions. "Non-detained" means what it says: not in ICE custody. Some of those convicted are serving sentences elsewhere and will walk out one day. Others are in the community. Others ICE cannot find. Across ICE's books as a whole, the agency counted 662,566 noncitizens with criminal convictions or charges. The figures were produced only because a congressman asked; there is no schedule for publishing them again.

The docket is the arithmetic of decades of under-resourced interior enforcement. The Congressional Research Service reports that it stood at 7.3 million cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including roughly 1.6 million aliens with final orders of removal. Working the criminal part of that backlog is arithmetic too. Internal ICE data obtained by NBC News show that from Oct. 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025, the agency arrested 752 people convicted of homicide, at most 6% of the known homicide convicts on its own docket, and 1,693 convicted of sexual assault, at most 11% of them. Even an administration committed to removing criminal aliens cannot detain the criminal docket with the beds and officers Congress has funded.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences, and Rising

The same pattern appears at the front end of the system. United States Sentencing Commission data show non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024: 21,304 people. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens.

The share is climbing. In FY2025, 28,886 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 44% of all individuals sentenced that year, and 92% of them were illegal aliens.

Nor is the federal docket made up only of immigration cases. Noncitizens accounted for 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking offenders sentenced in FY2024, nearly one in five.

Enforcement capacity, meanwhile, spent years moving the other way. The Government Accountability Office found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500 (GAO-24-107598, October 2024). The country did not run out of criminal aliens. It ran out of immigration enforcement.

## 3. What the Texas Record Actually Shows

Texas keeps the country's most complete record of the immigration status of people it arrests and convicts, and for a decade advocates have leaned on Texas Department of Public Safety data to claim that illegal aliens offend at lower rates than the native born. That claim is an artifact of how status is recorded, not of how crime is distributed.

Texas ascertains the immigration status of many offenders only after they are in custody, sometimes years into a sentence. Analyses that divide the convictions of identified illegal aliens by a population estimate treat the unidentified remainder as native born and systematically understate illegal-alien criminality. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies who re-examined the DPS records conclude that once delayed identification is accounted for, illegal aliens are convicted at higher rates than the general population for serious crimes in Texas, including homicide and sexual assault (Kennedy, Richwine and Camarota, October 2022).

Texas is not evidence that criminal aliens are rare. It is evidence of what a state can learn about criminal aliens when it asks the question.

## 4. Detainers Refused, With the Bodies Counted

Ibarra was released by New York police before ICE could lodge a detainer. That pattern is now quantified in federal data.

The Department of Homeland Security reported on Oct. 12, 2026 that New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026. Those detainers covered aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicides, 132 kidnappings, 1,017 sexual offenses, 9,502 assaults, 2,198 weapons offenses and 4,324 dangerous drug offenses. New York is the example, not the exception. ICE records produced to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2026 show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022 through Feb. 6, 2025, 52% of them in California alone (13,025), plus more than 1,400 instances in which jails failed to give ICE adequate notification of a release.

Cooperation, by contrast, compounds. Under Executive Order 14159, ICE has grown its 287(g) partnerships, which deputize state and local officers to perform immigration enforcement functions, by 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025, to 2,246 active agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026. By Oct. 15, 2026, ICE had signed 2,679 agreements covering 38 states and two territories. New York, meanwhile, has legislated against cooperation: a state law signed in May 2026 bars local police departments from partnering or cooperating with ICE, effective Aug. 25, 2026. Every one of those agreements is a memorandum, not a statute, and a future administration could cancel them.

## Recommendations

1. Fund criminal-alien detention. Appropriate detention capacity dedicated to the criminal cases on ICE's non-detained docket, beginning with the 13,099 homicide and 15,811 sexual assault convictions ICE has already identified, and direct DHS to prioritize them.

2. Condition federal funds on detainer compliance. Make law enforcement and criminal justice grants to state and local governments contingent on honoring ICE detainers and providing notice of release dates.

3. Expand and protect 287(g). Fund training and equipment for participating agencies, require DHS to offer agreements to every state, and shield participating agencies from state laws that bar cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

4. Require public reporting. Direct DHS to publish quarterly the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, detainers issued and declined by jurisdiction, and every release of a criminal alien from custody.

---

*Data appendix with full source lines and methodology notes accompanies this brief. Brett Kessler is senior fellow for immigration policy at the Founders' Square Institute.*
