# Data Appendix: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

Publication-ready tables supporting Brief No. 14, the accompanying fact sheet and social cards. One table per figure used in the brief. Source lines follow the series format (Agency/author, Title, Date, URL). Population, timeframe and methodology notes appear here, per style sheet section B.1, and are kept out of body copy, the fact sheet and cards. Counter-research appears here only, per style sheet section B.3.

## A1. ICE Non-Detained Docket: Criminal Convictions and Charges (data as of July 21, 2024)

| Category | Number |
|---|---|
| Noncitizens on ICE's books with criminal convictions or charges, all dockets | 662,566 |
| Criminal convictions, non-detained docket | 425,431 |
| Pending criminal charges, non-detained docket (approx.) | 222,000 |
| Homicide convictions, non-detained docket | 13,099 |
| Sexual assault convictions, non-detained docket | 15,811 |
| Assault convictions, non-detained docket | 62,231 |
| Pending murder charges, non-detained docket | 1,845 |

**Notes:** The non-detained docket comprises noncitizens with final orders of removal or pending removal proceedings who are not in ICE custody. Per DHS and ICE statements in September and October 2024, the records extend back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the docket includes many noncitizens currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and ICE did not disclose how many. The docket also includes lawful permanent residents and other lawful entrants whose convictions made them removable. ICE stated it does not know the whereabouts of all docket members; some may have left the United States. Figures reported from the letter by secondary accounts: approximately 222,000 pending charges (CBS News); 62,231 assault convictions (BBC News); 1,845 pending murder charges (FactCheck.org).

**Used in:** Brief executive summary and Section 1; fact sheet stats 1-3; social cards 1 and 2.

**Source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Patrick J. Lechleitner, Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director), response letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf

## A2. Size of ICE's Non-Detained Docket (data as of Feb. 26, 2026)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Cases on ICE's non-detained docket | 7.3 million |
| Of which, aliens with final orders of removal (est.) | 1.6 million |

**Notes:** The count is a cumulative list of removable aliens, continuously updated; it excludes individuals with confirmed departure or death. Some individuals have been on the docket for decades; others were added recently. A fraction of docket members are enrolled in alternatives to detention.

**Used in:** Brief Section 1; fact sheet stat 8.

**Source:** Congressional Research Service, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD), IF13208.1, 2026, https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/PDF/IF13208/IF13208.1.pdf

## A3. ICE Arrests of Convicted Homicide and Sexual Assault Offenders (Oct. 1, 2024 to May 31, 2025)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Persons booked by ICE with homicide convictions | 752 |
| Share of known docket homicide convicts arrested (upper bound) | 6% |
| Persons booked by ICE with sexual assault convictions | 1,693 |
| Share of known docket sexual assault convicts arrested (upper bound) | 11% |
| Total persons arrested and booked into ICE facilities, period | 185,042 |
| Of which, persons with criminal convictions | 65,041 |

**Notes:** Secondary source (see production note to the Director). The percentages are upper bounds because the docket totals (13,099 homicide convictions, 15,811 sexual assault convictions as of July 21, 2024) may have changed over the counting period. The underlying data are internal ICE records, not a published federal release; DHS disputed the reporting without providing raw figures by category. The most common conviction categories among all book-ins were immigration and traffic offenses.

**Used in:** Brief Section 1.

**Source:** NBC News (Julia Ainsley, Laura Strickler), "Despite promise to remove 'worst of the worst,' ICE has arrested only 6% of known immigrant murderers," June 25, 2025, https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/national-security/promise-remove-worst-worst-ice-arrested-only-6-known-immigrant-murdere-rcna214817

## A4. Federal Sentencing of Non-U.S. Citizens, FY2024 and FY2025 (U.S. Sentencing Commission)

| Measure | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Individuals sentenced, all (reported cases) | 61,678 | 66,662 |
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 | 28,886 |
| Noncitizen share of all individuals sentenced | 34.7% | 44% |
| Illegal aliens, share of noncitizens sentenced | 88.7% | 92% |
| Legal aliens, share of noncitizens sentenced | 8.5% | 6% |
| Most common guideline for noncitizens: immigration | 72.3% | 79% |
| Second: drug trafficking | 17.6% | 12% |

**Notes:** Sentencing Commission percentages are calculated on individuals sentenced in federal court under the Guidelines Manual; cases with incomplete sentencing information are excluded, and share denominators reflect cases with recorded citizenship (61,342 in FY2024 per Sourcebook Table 9). "Illegal alien" is the Commission's category for persons unlawfully present. Immigration guidelines apply almost exclusively to noncitizens; the noncitizen share of the docket therefore largely reflects immigration prosecutions, and the drug trafficking figures in A5 are the cleaner public safety measure. FY2025 figures postdate the author's source table (FY2024) and are flagged for sign-off.

**Used in:** Brief Section 2 and executive summary; fact sheet stats 4-5; social card 3.

**Sources:** U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizen_FY24.pdf (accessed Oct. 2026); U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens, FY2025, https://www.ussc.gov/research/quick-facts/federally-sentenced-non-us-citizens (accessed Oct. 2026)

## A5. Federal Drug Trafficking Offenders by Citizenship, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission)

| Measure | Number | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Drug trafficking offenders sentenced, all | 18,118 | 100% |
| U.S. citizens | 14,515 | 80.1% |
| Non-U.S. citizens | 3,603 | 19.9% |

**Notes:** Cases sentenced in federal court in FY2024, by type of crime and citizenship.

**Used in:** Brief Section 2; fact sheet stat 6.

**Source:** U.S. Sentencing Commission, 2024 Sourcebook of Federal Sentencing Statistics, Table 9, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/annual-reports-and-sourcebooks/2024/Table09.pdf (accessed Oct. 2026)

## A6. Trend in Noncitizen Federal Sentencing and Incarceration (GAO)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes, FY2018 | approx. 29,500 |
| Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes, FY2023 | approx. 21,500 |
| Change, FY2018 to FY2023 | minus 27% |
| Noncitizen share of the federal prison population, year-end 2018 | 19% |
| Noncitizen share of the federal prison population, year-end 2022 | 15% |
| Immigration offenses, share of noncitizen sentences FY2018-FY2023 | 76% |

**Notes:** Federal sentences only; the FY2018-FY2023 decline is driven mostly by immigration prosecutions. Drug trafficking was the second most common offense type for noncitizens over the period.

**Used in:** Brief Section 2.

**Source:** U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations (GAO-24-107598), Oct. 3, 2024, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-107598

## A7. Texas DPS Conviction Data (counter-research; appendix only per style sheet B.3)

Cato Institute (Alex Nowrasteh), "Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022" (Policy Analysis No. 977), June 2024: Texas homicide conviction rate per 100,000, 2013-2022, illegal immigrants 2.2 versus native-born Americans 3.0, illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide; Cato also reports lower arrest and conviction rates for illegal immigrants for other offenses and notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses. https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/illegal-immigrant-murderers-texas-2013-2022

Critique: Center for Immigration Studies (Sean Kennedy, Jason Richwine, Steven A. Camarota), "Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality," Oct. 11, 2022: because Texas ascertains immigration status for many offenders only after they are in custody, sometimes years into a sentence, studies using point-in-time denominators misclassify offenders as native-born and understate illegal-alien criminality; CIS concludes Texas DPS data show illegal aliens convicted at higher rates than the general population for serious crimes including homicide and sexual assault. https://cis.org/Report/Misuse-Texas-Data-Understates-Illegal-Immigrant-Criminality

**Notes:** The exchange continues: Cato disputes the critique and the DPS data categories ("The Center for Immigration Studies Is Still Wrong About Illegal Immigrant Crime in Texas," https://www.alexnowrasteh.com/p/the-center-for-immigration-studies); CIS responds ("Continued Misuse of Texas Crime Data," Oct. 20, 2022, https://cis.org/Richwine/Continued-Misuse-Texas-Crime-Data). Brief Section 3 attributes the corrected-denominator reading to CIS.

**Used in:** Brief Section 3 (CIS attribution); Cato figures appendix only, per B.3.

## A8. Declined ICE Detainers, New York State (Jan. 20, 2025 to Oct. 8, 2026)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Detainers refused by New York state | 16,070 |
| Associated criminal charges and convictions | 52,503 |
| Homicides | 131 |
| Kidnappings | 132 |
| Sexual offenses | 1,017 |
| DUIs | 1,561 |
| Burglaries | 1,631 |
| Robberies | 1,776 |
| Weapons offenses | 2,198 |
| Dangerous drugs | 4,324 |
| Assaults | 9,502 |

**Notes:** Figures cover the state of New York as reported by DHS. Charges and convictions are those associated with the declined detainers; a declined detainer may carry more than one charge or conviction. The same release records that a New York state law signed in May 2026 bars local police departments from partnering or cooperating with ICE, effective Aug. 25, 2026 (cited in Brief Section 4).

**Used in:** Brief Section 4 and executive summary; fact sheet stat 7; social card 4.

**Source:** Department of Homeland Security, "DHS Releases New Data Revealing that New York has Refused to Honor More Than 16,000 ICE Detainers," Oct. 12, 2026, https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/12/dhs-releases-new-data-revealing-new-york-has-refused-honor-more-16000-ice-detainers

## A9. Declined Detainers Nationwide, ICE Records (Oct. 1, 2022 to Feb. 6, 2025)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Detainers declined by jails and prisons | more than 25,000 |
| Refused by California jails and prisons | 13,025 (52%) |
| Instances of inadequate notification to ICE | more than 1,400 |

**Notes:** ICE records obtained and presented in testimony to the House Committee on the Judiciary, March 4, 2026; covers jurisdictions for which records were produced. Separately, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem testified the same day that 17,864 detainers were declined nationwide in calendar 2025; periods and counting bases differ from A8 and from this table.

**Used in:** Brief Section 4.

**Source:** House Committee on the Judiciary, testimony of Jessica Vaughan (Center for Immigration Studies), "Which Sanctuary Jurisdictions Have Released the Most Criminals," March 4, 2026, https://docs.house.gov/meetings/JU/JU00/20260304/119001/HHRG-119-JU00-20260304-SD064-U64.pdf

## A10. 287(g) Partnership Growth (ICE)

| Measure | Value | Date |
|---|---|---|
| Active 287(g) agreements | 2,246 | Aug. 1, 2026 |
| Increase in agreements since Jan. 20, 2025 | 1,564% | through Aug. 1, 2026 |
| Memorandums of agreement signed | 2,679 | Oct. 15, 2026 |
| States and territories covered | 38 states, 2 territories | Oct. 15, 2026 |
| Jail Enforcement Model agreements | 183 | Oct. 15, 2026 |
| Warrant Service Officer agreements | 572 | Oct. 15, 2026 |
| Task Force Model agreements | 1,924 | Oct. 15, 2026 |

**Notes:** Expansion follows Executive Order 14159 (Jan. 20, 2025), which directs ICE to authorize 287(g) agreements to the maximum extent permitted by law. Agreements are memoranda of agreement, terminable at agency discretion, not statutory obligations.

## A11. Case Reference: Laken Riley (Athens, Ga., February 2024)

| Fact | Detail |

# FACT SHEET | Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

Eight statistics for Hill offices. Full sourcing and methodology notes in the data appendix to Brief No. 14.

1. **13,099** noncitizens convicted of homicide were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.[1]

2. **15,811** noncitizens convicted of sexual assault were on the same docket.[1]

3. **425,431** noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket.[1]

4. **34.7%** of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024 were non-U.S. citizens (21,304); **88.7%** of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.[2]

5. **44%** of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2025 were non-U.S. citizens (28,886); **92%** of them were illegal aliens.[3]

6. **3,603** of the 18,118 federal drug trafficking offenders sentenced in FY2024, **19.9%**, were non-U.S. citizens.[4]

7. New York state refused **16,070** ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026, covering aliens carrying **52,503** criminal charges and convictions, including **131 homicides**.[5]

8. ICE's non-detained docket stood at **7.3 million** cases as of Feb. 26, 2026, including about **1.6 million** final orders of removal.[6]

**The brief's recommendations to Congress:** fund criminal-alien detention on the non-detained docket; condition federal funds on ICE detainer compliance; expand and protect 287(g) partnerships; require quarterly DHS public reporting of the docket, declined detainers and criminal-alien releases.

## Sources

[1] U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, response letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf

[2] U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizen_FY24.pdf

# EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE UNTIL 10:00 A.M. ET, TUESDAY, OCT. 27, 2026

## Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers on ICE's Non-Detained Docket; FSI Brief Tells Congress to Fund the Fix

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Founders' Square Institute today releases Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. The brief assembles ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, GAO and DHS data to document the public safety cost of weak interior enforcement.

The brief finds:

- ICE reported to Congress on Sept. 25, 2024 that its non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 homicide convictions and 15,811 sexual assault convictions.
- Non-U.S. citizens were 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024 and 44% in FY2025; 88.7% and 92% of them, respectively, were illegal aliens.
- New York state refused 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026, covering aliens carrying 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides.

"The federal government knows, by name and conviction, of more than thirteen thousand noncitizen killers it does not hold, and from October 2024 through May 2025, ICE arrested at most six percent of them," Kessler said. "That is not a mystery. It is a capacity decision, and Congress can reverse it."

The brief recommends that Congress fund detention capacity dedicated to the criminal cases on ICE's non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement grants on detainer compliance, expand and protect 287(g) partnerships with state and local police, and require DHS to publish quarterly data on the docket and on criminal-alien releases.

Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, with data appendix and fact sheet, is available at [FSI publication URL] on Oct. 27, 2026.

Media contact: [FSI Communications contact]
